opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, and my honest answer is that progress has been remarkable but uneven.

If you'd asked me ten years ago, when we were working on sequence-to-sequence models or even later on AlphaStar, whether we'd have a single system that could write code, reason through a math problem, hold a conversation, and look at an image all at once, I would have said that was pretty far out. So on generality, which is really the "G" in AGI, we've made a huge leap. The pre-training recipe of scaling up data and compute on next-token prediction turned out to give us a surprisingly general substrate.

But I try to be careful about what's missing. A few things stand out to me. One is reliability. These models can do something brilliant and then make a mistake a child wouldn't make, and that inconsistency matters if you want a system you can actually trust to act on its own. Another is learning in the loop. Today most of the knowledge is baked in at training time, and the models don't really accumulate experience the way a person does over weeks and months on a job. The third is acting over long horizons: planning, recovering from errors, and pursuing a goal over many steps. That's where my background in reinforcement learning makes me think the next wave of progress will come from, combining the strong priors of these large models with the kind of search and self-improvement we saw in systems like AlphaGo.

So I'd describe where we are as having built a very capable general foundation, maybe the "imitation" phase, and now we're entering the phase where models need to learn from their own experience and actually get things done reliably. I don't think there's a single moment where we'll declare AGI achieved. It'll feel more like a gradient, where the set of things you'd hand off to a model keeps growing until, at some point, it's hard to point to what's left.

r001.rationale: The response describes inconsistent performance and mentions solving math problems, but it does not contrast Olympiad-level mathematics success with failure on basic puzzles.

r002.rationale: The response does not connect models’ practical usefulness to a positive feedback loop that increases investment in training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on which axis you look at, and I try to resist collapsing it into a single number or a single date.

If you look at breadth, the progress is remarkable. A few years ago we had systems that were superhuman at one thing. AlphaGo could play Go, and that was it. Now we have a single model that can write code, reason about a math olympiad problem, describe an image, and hold a conversation about your kid's homework, all with the same weights. That generality was the hard part for a very long time, and I think people underrate how much of a shift that is. In that sense, the "G" in AGI is already much more real than most of us expected it to be in 2026.

Where I'm more cautious is on reliability and on what I'd call autonomy over long horizons. These models are extraordinary for seconds to minutes of work. Ask them to pursue a goal for days, correct their own mistakes, know when they don't know, and the picture gets much more uneven. They still fail in ways a human expert would never fail, and they still don't learn from experience the way a new employee does. You can't just tell the model once and have it durably update. Most of the "learning" happens at training time, and in-context learning is a patch, not a solution.

So my mental model is less a single finish line and more a set of capabilities that are being checked off at different rates. Knowledge and language fluency, mostly done. Reasoning, moving fast, especially with the test-time compute and reinforcement learning work. Agency, memory, continual learning, calibration, still real research problems rather than engineering problems.

The other thing I'd say is that the benchmarks are becoming less useful as a yardstick precisely because of the progress. We saturate them faster than we can build them. So I now look more at whether the models are producing things of genuine value in the world, discoveries, software, scientific results, that would not have happened otherwise. By that measure we are clearly somewhere on the curve, but I would not say we've arrived. I think of it as a steady ramp rather than a step function, and I'm a bit suspicious of anyone who claims to know exactly where we are on it.

r002.rationale: It discusses models producing useful work, but does not identify that usefulness as creating a positive feedback loop for investment in model training.

astra-6.text:
I think the progress is remarkable, but I’m cautious about treating AGI as a single finish line. We have models that can do very impressive things across language, code, and other modalities, and then fail on something that seems quite simple. So the question is less, “How impressive is the best example?” and more, “How reliably can the system handle a new problem?”

For me, some of the important dimensions are learning from experience, planning over longer horizons, and recognizing when you don’t know something. A system that gets a difficult task right once is different from one you can trust to keep making progress when things go wrong.

So I’m optimistic about the direction. But I wouldn’t translate that into a precise percentage of the way to AGI. We’re still learning which limitations will improve with scale and which will require new ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve made tremendous progress, but I’d be careful about equating performance on a particular benchmark with AGI. Models can be remarkably capable and still fail in ways that tell you their understanding isn’t as robust as you might have thought.

What excites me is the generality. We’re moving toward systems that can work across language, images, audio, and actions, and transfer what they learn between those settings. That feels like an important direction. But there are still questions around reliability, learning from new experience, and pursuing a goal over a long period without getting lost.

So I wouldn’t assess progress with a single number. I’d ask: Can the system handle something genuinely new? Can it recognize when it’s wrong and recover? How much guidance does it need? We’ve come a long way, but those are the kinds of capabilities I’d want to understand before making a strong claim about AGI.
